dv/dt and di/dt are voltage/current rates; capacitive coupling, insulation stress, inductive spikes and EMI are correctly distinguished.

General conclusion that higher damping means faster settling is false beyond critical damping: the overdamped dominant pole approaches zero as damping increases, slowing the response.

Zero-cross closing may reduce a voltage step but magnetic/inductive history can defeat the benefit; explicit qualification avoids a universal switching rule.
Harmonics are a hypothesis, with loading, mounting and voltage alternatives plus spectrum/temperature checks; temporal coincidence is explicitly not proof.

Simple parallel LC resonance cancels input susceptance while branch currents circulate, increasing input impedance and reducing source current compared with series resonance; not every local current is a maximum.
At comparable converter loading, larger source harmonic impedance generally yields larger voltage distortion for a similar injected spectrum; usually qualification avoids a universal spectrum claim.

STATCOM/SVC dynamic reactive/voltage control is correctly distinguished from fixed support as a capability, not guaranteed system-wide stability.
Series resonance cancels reactance in one path; parallel resonance cancels reactive input current while branch currents may be large. Resistance limits both effects, correctly qualified.
Specified few-cycle energization current is plausibly transformer inrush; unfavorable initial flux and settling explain the given case without a universal decay-time claim.
Ringing alone does not establish source instability; local RLC, wiring and measurement hypotheses correctly remain open.
Current continuity, stray inductance/capacitance and recovery effects explain inverter switching peaks; gate/layout/snubber controls are qualitative without invented safe settings.
Ideal transformer plus series loss/leakage and shunt excitation/loss elements is a complete introductory terminal model; explicitly scoped to the questions/model rather than all magnetic detail.
Make-break bounce changes initial stored energy repeatedly and can produce spikes/arcing/ringing; possible effects are qualified and not a measured universal waveform.
First-order small-drop line relation (P*R+Q*X)/V is explicitly approximate; W*ohm/V and var*ohm/V both have voltage dimensions under consistent per-phase definitions.
Basic simulation workflow correctly supplies circuit values or a transfer function and checks frequency/transient response; this does not claim simulation alone validates a real build.
Passband, stopband and transition definitions are complete introductory amplitude-response descriptions.
Fast sweeps can miss steady state and blur/shift an apparent peak without changing the fixed circuit's natural frequency; explicit circuit/damping/measurement conditions retained.
Supply connection selection is conditional on load, voltage, grounding and neutral needs; wye is preferred, not the only possible neutral arrangement.
Introductory explanation correctly retains historical/regional standardization and engineering compromises; it does not claim a uniquely optimal derivation of 50 or 60 Hz.
Changing L/C reactance redistributes complex branch currents and voltages; response and cancellation are correctly circuit dependent rather than universally monotone.
Ideal series impedance is R+j*(XL-XC), with XL and XC understood as positive reactance magnitudes; algebra and sign agree with j*omega*L+1/(j*omega*C).
Generator/drive distortion and regulation stress are conditional on source impedance, size, load mix and filters; no guaranteed fault or spectrum.
Free natural response and forced-frequency resonance are correctly separated while connected through the circuit dynamics; no identity between damped ringing and every resonance frequency.
AFE versus reactor/filter choice retains network, emissions, cost and operating conditions; explicitly rejects blanket replacement and avoids numeric performance guarantees.
For conventional balanced three-phase sinusoids, changing 50 to 60 Hz preserves 120-degree geometry and sqrt(3) connection factors while altering reactance and machine design.
Initial capacitor voltage, inductor current, flux and source phase govern switching response; examples are conditional and do not invent an initial value.
Feasible steady-state load flow is explicitly not proof of dynamic stability; reactive reserves and margins can identify vulnerability with further study.
No-load transformer excitation has flux-producing magnetizing current and in-phase core-loss current, correctly represented by the shunt branch.
Voltage and power have different units; resistor average power V_rms^2/R also depends on load, so RMS voltage is not itself power.
Bounce/chatter creates repeated make-break events that can launch transients; conditional stress explanation is complete.
Quoted zero net reactance is paraphrased correctly with an explicit series-RLC example and resistance-limited source response.
Lower upstream THD may reflect aggregation/cancellation or a larger fundamental denominator; answer correctly offers hypotheses, not a unique source proof.
5th/7th dominant components are explicitly assigned to a six-pulse converter, and resulting RMS/loss effects are qualitative.
Transient is the unsettled response after a change, with possible surge/overshoot/ringing before steady behavior; brief is relative to settling, not explicitly less than one AC cycle.
Rolloff is attenuation slope in dB per octave/decade outside a cutoff region; complete low-risk definition.
Balanced three currents and spatially displaced motor windings produce a rotating fundamental field; a single unassisted winding produces pulsation rather than that field.

Triplen means integer multiples of three, not only odd multiples; even triplen harmonics can exist without half-wave symmetry. The correct neutral-addition mechanism does not cure the incomplete definition.

Delta connection does not generally authorize continued operation with a damaged phase; open-delta transformer operation has specific ratings/topology and cannot be generalized to an arbitrary delta load or phase failure.
Apparent minus real power is not reactive power: S^2=P^2+Q^2 in the sinusoidal case, and dissipated wheel-slip energy is real power. The analogy teaches the wrong physical relationship.
Power-flow methods can be unbalanced and faults can be solved in phase coordinates; balanced power-flow assumption and required sequence-only analysis are falsely universal.
Constant power alone does not guarantee longer equipment life, absent flicker or smooth motor torque; system, load and regulated variable are unspecified.
Reversal applies to swapping two phase supply conductors of a suitable directly supplied motor; arbitrary two wires or drive/control connections are not a complete operational instruction.
Bonding/discharge requirements need applicable code, capacitor class and specified discharge means/time; grounding is not proof of discharged safe maintenance state.
Equivalent circuit is unspecified in the question, while answer assumes transformer copper/core-loss behavior; half-load output also requires power factor and voltage definition.
Software for this refers to an absent prior task; list of power-system tools cannot establish the missing question context.
Soft-start and reactive compensation distinction is useful, but capacitors are not universally still needed: compensation depends on running load and can use other devices or none.
Reactive supply/reserve deficit can depress voltage, whereas reduced inductive demand can raise it; reactive power drops too low lacks location, sign and demand/supply definition.
Motor type and excitation source are unspecified; permanent-magnet or DC-excited machines need not draw grid reactive power to establish their fields.

Practical mains/drive multimeter and oscilloscope advice omits instrument/probe voltage-category and isolation/grounding constraints; true RMS is an accuracy property, not electrical safety assurance.
Start/run power-factor ranges and decreasing reactive demand require motor type, loading and source evidence; generic motor wording cannot support these numerical ranges.
kVAR correction relation is not capacitance: voltage, frequency, phase connection and initial lag/lead convention are also necessary. No numeric capacitor size can be verified from the supplied data.
Capacitor-placement guidance omits harmonic resonance, switching and overcompensation checks; a low-voltage bus alone is insufficient placement evidence.
Increasing resistance lowers Q in a series resonator but increasing parallel shunt resistance raises Q; topology and response variable are missing from the universal damping/bandwidth claim.
Protection device list is conditional, but prevents catastrophic failures is a guarantee not established by device presence; equipment and coordination ratings remain absent.
Conventional compensation of a lagging load can reduce upstream RMS current and feeder drop at fixed real power; can improve language does not guarantee stability or unlimited compensation.
Overshoot alone is not a design-failure diagnosis; expected dynamics, parasitics, probing and actual component limits remain necessary evidence.
Scope time-domain timing/peak/ringing versus RMS averaging distinction is sound; explanatory comparison is not an instruction to connect an unsafe probe.
Parallel branch phasors can be large and opposing while their vector sum is modest; KCL cancellation correctly distinguishes branch and source currents.
Conventional fixed-coefficient discrete LTI FIR response is finite and BIBO stable; IIR recursion can be unstable, and linear phase is possible for appropriate FIR symmetry, not every filter.
Brief peaks can violate voltage/rate limits or cause EMI even with low average energy; repeated stress is conditional and no guaranteed failure threshold is invented.
Filter class is conditional on noise and useful-signal bands; basic low-pass/notch/band-pass distinction is correct without promising recovery of overlapping signal/noise spectra.
Balanced fifth harmonic phase advances by 5*120 degrees, equivalent to negative-sequence rotation; conditional motor loss/heating/torque consequences are consistent.
10 V RMS and 10 V DC across the same constant resistor both produce 100/R W; explicitly confines equivalent effect to appropriate resistive heating rather than all loads.
Listed capacitor breakdown, pressure, capacitance and ESR failures are plausible conditional mechanisms; protection list does not guarantee safety or provide unsourced settings.
Fixed-point coefficient changes can shift poles/zeros and response; stability sensitivity is especially relevant to recursive filters and is not stated to affect every FIR alike.
Stored magnetic energy and current continuity explain opening-switch arcing/spikes with conditional magnitude; discharge path and interruption rate matter.
Basic material impedance can have resistive and capacitive frequency-dependent behavior; bioimpedance is an application, with no diagnostic recommendation or performance claim.

Conventional grid-connected synchronous generator excitation controls reactive exchange at a fixed operating point; greater excitation raises internal EMF and supplied Q in this standard introductory setting.
Conventional sinusoidal complex-power components satisfy |S|^2=P^2+Q^2 and PF=P/|S|; kVA denotes apparent magnitude while vector-sum wording expresses the underlying P+jQ construction.
Positive L/C tolerances lower 1/sqrt(LC); high-Q narrow bandwidth makes the resulting shift more significant. Nominal formula is explicitly not exact measured frequency.
Need for detailed studies is explicitly conditional on plant complexity, load and expansion; does not waive mandatory protection or connection requirements.
Flicker, hot capacitors and high THD suggest multiple possibilities; voltage fluctuation and resonance/overload are distinguished and measurement context remains required.
High Q is associated with narrower, sharper resonance and lower dissipation in the described resonator comparison; no universal topology-specific resistor claim.

Independent sine integrations give RMS/peak=1/sqrt(2), reciprocal sqrt(2), peak-to-peak twice peak, full-cycle signed average zero; rectified average is distinguished and waveform restriction explicit.
Underdamped stable circuit response has decaying oscillatory poles and can ring/overshoot; introductory slowly wording is qualitative rather than a universal settling-time comparison.
Missing dramatic peak does not disprove reactive cancellation; topology, response variable, Q, source impedance and measurement confounds explicitly remain.
Motor temperature alone does not prove harmonics; loading, ventilation, unbalance and mechanical alternatives remain, with measurements needed.
High-Q narrow notch is limited by tolerances and practical implementation; answer does not guarantee a numeric achievable bandwidth or every filter's instability.
Explicit same-frequency sinusoidal steady-state phasors retain magnitude and relative phase, often RMS, while suppressing time variation; complete introductory explanation.
Variable inverter-connected resources can alter flows, harmonics and support requirements; often and sometimes qualifications avoid claiming all renewable installations require storage.
Fault is an abnormal electrical condition; transient is a temporary response that may follow normal switching as well as faults. Correct distinction.
Identical RMS gives equal average constant-resistor heating while waveform peaks/spectra can affect other equipment differently; does not generalize resistor equivalence to all devices.
Ideal inductive impedance j*omega*L rotates voltage 90 degrees ahead of current under the conventional positive-frequency phasor convention; magnitude and sign are correct.
High-Q series resonance can magnify element voltages and source current, with heating/insulation consequences conditional; also correctly identifies useful controlled applications.
High Q alone is not instability: a stable passive resonator can have high Q and decaying ringing. Generic reduce gain/damp diagnosis has neither topology nor observed behavior evidence.
PF=400/500=0.8 is correct, but PF is not useful-work efficiency; 300 var magnitude additionally requires sinusoidal assumptions and neither Q sign nor inductive load follows from P and S alone.
Balanced fundamental and balanced triplen loads can produce neutral current; nonzero neutral current is not proof of fundamental imbalance and its magnitude is not a general scalar imbalance measure.

Even treating 100 hp as 75 kW electrical input, Qc=75*(sqrt(1-0.75^2)/0.75-sqrt(1-0.95^2)/0.95)=41.4924 kvar, outside 35-40. Motor horsepower is mechanical output and requires efficiency for input kW, worsening the sizing error.

Possibly qualification helps, but low mechanical output is not low electrical real power because losses consume real power. Hot/light-load motor diagnosis requires measured current, input power, loading and loss context.
0.95-1.05 pu target and suggested capacitor/tap action need equipment, jurisdiction, bus base and operating limit evidence; low voltage alone does not identify reactive support as the remedy.
Motor nameplate kW normally denotes shaft output, not electrical input real power; efficiency is missing. 5/0.85 is only valid if 5 kW explicitly denotes input power.
In this context references an absent circuit/prior discussion; generic clamp/snubber comparison cannot establish standalone context completeness.
PF 0.7 alone does not establish excessive current for the motor's load, utility penalty or a safe capacitor solution; rating/loading, tariff and harmonic/switching conditions are missing.
Location tradeoff omits motor-side self-excitation, switching/interlocking and harmonic compatibility; not a complete installation recommendation for an unspecified motor/drive.
Natural undamped frequency, damped free-oscillation frequency and forced response peak can differ; response variable/damping must be specified before same-idea wording is reliable.
Reactive supply/demand sign and network location are absent; voltage-control intuition is useful but blanket long-line support statement ignores light-load capacitive charging and stability criteria.
Referred impedance influences regulation, but increasing reactance need not increase drop for leading power-factor load; load sign and operating conditions need qualification.
THD denominator is fundamental RMS current, not arbitrary total current flowing now; TDD reference demand definition also needs the applicable measurement standard/context.
The model is not identified in the question; transformer, feeder/source impedance and fault assumptions cannot be supplied solely by the answer.
Voltage regulation improvement is not proof of dynamic stability, and proper engineering cannot itself guarantee net benefit without study; compensation topology/operating case is absent.
Universal typical 10-20 year capacitor lifespan lacks type, environment and supporting evidence; moisture/thermal degradation is plausible but does not establish that range.
Added motor reactive demand depends on motor type/excitation and operating load; a synchronous or converter-fed machine can have zero/leading demand, so generic increase is not established.
Plus/minus 10 percent acceptability for most impedance studies lacks study sensitivity and evidence; measured values are not automatically more accurate without frequency, uncertainty and method.

Identical linear branch impedance keeps its angle across ideal wye/delta, but changed winding voltage/loading in real equipment can change power factor; load/voltage assumptions absent from unconditional no.

Discharge time and safe residual voltage depend on RC and applicable requirements; within minutes/required by codes lacks values/code applicability, and presence of a resistor is not proof of discharge.

Absolute high P and Q do not establish high relative stress or significant drop without voltage, impedance, capacity and loading baselines; reinforcement need cannot be inferred from magnitudes alone.
P-angle and Q-magnitude decoupling is an approximation for predominantly inductive networks; bus voltage phasors need known network admittances/topology to determine flows, not voltages alone.
Unbalance definition must reference balanced 120-degree phase spacing rather than matching angles; transient also includes oscillatory events, not solely a fast spike/impulse.
Phase-sequence reversal applies to appropriate directly supplied machines; any two phases is not a general instruction for drive-controlled outputs or arbitrary equipment.
Utility meter capabilities, true versus displacement factor and billing aggregation depend on meter/tariff; real/reactive channels alone do not universally establish true PF for distorted currents.
